questions.q: For f(x) = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx + c with symmetric invertible H, where is the critical point?
questions.x: Setting ∇f = Hx + b = 0 gives the critical point x* = −H⁻¹b.

questions.q: At a critical point the Hessian is H = [[2,1],[1,2]]. Classify the point.
questions.x: The eigenvalues of [[2,1],[1,2]] are 1 and 3, both positive, so H is positive definite and the point is a strict local minimum.

questions.q: Match each Hessian eigenvalue pattern at a critical point to its classification
questions.x: Positive definite H gives a strict minimum, negative definite a strict maximum, indefinite a saddle, and a singular semidefinite H calls for higher-order or linear-term information.

questions.q: For f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx with H positive definite and b ≠ 0, the principal axes of the elliptical contours lie along
questions.a: Eigenvectors of H, through the critical point
w: Eigenvectors of H, through the origin
The coordinate axes x₁ and x₂, through the origin
The gradient direction at the starting point x₀
questions.x: Contours are ellipses centred at x* = −H⁻¹b, with principal axes along the eigenvectors of H passing through x*.

questions.q: For a positive definite quadratic, along which direction are the elliptical contours most elongated?
questions.a: The eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue
w: The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue
The eigenvector with eigenvalue closest to one
The direction of the linear term b
questions.x: Along eigenvector vᵢ the level set has semi-axis proportional to 1/√λᵢ, so the smallest eigenvalue gives the longest axis.

questions.q: f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx with H = [[2,2],[2,2]] and b = (1,−1). Which statement is true?
w: A line of minimizers runs along (1,−1)
A unique minimum lies at x* = −H⁻¹b
A line of minimizers runs along the direction (1,1)
questions.x: The null space of H is spanned by (1,−1), and bᵀ(1,−1) = 2, so f = 2α along x = α(1,−1) and f decreases linearly toward −∞ as α → −∞.

questions.q: H = [[2,2],[2,2]] and b = (1,1). What is the minimum structure of f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx?
questions.a: A line of minimizers parallel to (1,−1)
w: A unique minimizer at the origin
A line of minimizers parallel to the direction (1,1)
questions.x: b lies in the range of H, so Hx = −b has the whole line x₁ + x₂ = −½ as solutions, all sharing the same minimum value.

questions.q: Find and classify the critical point of f(x,y) = x² − y² + 2x.
questions.x: ∇f = (2x + 2, −2y) vanishes at (−1, 0), and the Hessian diag(2, −2) is indefinite, so the point is a saddle.

questions.q: A search direction p at x is a descent direction when
questions.x: A descent direction has negative directional derivative ∇f(x)ᵀp < 0, so f decreases for small enough α > 0.

questions.q: State the Armijo sufficient decrease condition for step α along p.
questions.x: Armijo requires the actual decrease to be at least a fraction c₁ of the decrease predicted by the linear model, f(x+αp) ≤ f(x) + c₁α∇fᵀp.

questions.q: State the (weak) Wolfe curvature condition with constant c₂.
questions.x: The curvature condition requires the slope at the new point to rise to at least c₂ times the initial (negative) slope, which excludes overly short steps.

questions.q: Typical Wolfe constants for a Newton or quasi-Newton line search are
questions.x: The constants satisfy 0 < c₁ < c₂ < 1, with c₁ = 10⁻⁴ and c₂ = 0.9 typical for Newton and quasi-Newton (c₂ = 0.1 for nonlinear CG).

questions.q: Steepest descent on f = ½xᵀHx, H = diag(1, 2), from x₀ = (1, 1). What step does an exact line search give?
questions.x: With g = (1, 2), gᵀg = 5 and gᵀHg = 1 + 8 = 9, so α = gᵀg/(gᵀHg) = 5/9.

questions.q: Steepest descent with exact line search on a quadratic with condition number κ = 9. Worst-case reduction factor of f − f* per iteration?
questions.x: The worst-case factor is ((κ−1)/(κ+1))² = (8/10)² = 0.64, so a large condition number slows steepest descent.

questions.q: Put the steps of a backtracking (Armijo) line search in order
steps: Choose an initial step α (α = 1 for Newton-type methods)
If the check fails, set α ← ρα with 0 < ρ < 1 and re-check
Accept α and update x ← x + αp
questions.x: Backtracking starts from a full step and contracts α by a factor ρ until sufficient decrease holds, then accepts that step.

questions.q: Why does steepest descent with exact line search zigzag in a narrow valley?
questions.a: Successive gradients are orthogonal to each other
w: Successive gradients are parallel to each other
The exact step overshoots the minimum along p_k
The Hessian of a quadratic changes along each line
questions.x: Exact line search makes ∇f(x_{k+1})ᵀp_k = 0, so consecutive steepest descent directions meet at right angles.

questions.q: With gradient g and Hessian H, the Newton step is
questions.x: Newton's step minimizes the local quadratic model, giving Hp = −g, so p = −H⁻¹g.

questions.q: Pure Newton (α = 1) on a strictly convex quadratic converges in
questions.a: One iteration, from any starting point
w: n iterations for an n-dimensional problem
Two iterations, from any starting point
One iteration, only near the minimizer
questions.x: The quadratic model equals f exactly, so x − H⁻¹g lands on the minimizer in a single step from anywhere.

questions.q: The Newton direction is guaranteed to be a descent direction when
w: H is merely nonsingular and symmetric
questions.x: gᵀp = −gᵀH⁻¹g, which is negative for every nonzero g when H is positive definite.

questions.q: A modified Newton method handles an indefinite Hessian by
questions.a: Adding τI so that H + τI is positive definite
w: Replacing H by its transpose and solving again for the step
Flipping the sign of the gradient before solving Hp = −g
Using a fixed step length of one in place of a line search
questions.x: Modified Newton adds a multiple of the identity (or modifies eigenvalues or a Cholesky factor) so the step solves (H + τI)p = −g with a positive definite matrix.

questions.q: With s = x_{k+1} − x_k and y = g_{k+1} − g_k, the BFGS update satisfies which secant condition?
questions.x: BFGS chooses B_{k+1} so that B_{k+1}s = y, matching the observed change in gradient along the last step.

questions.q: Which condition keeps the BFGS approximation positive definite?
questions.a: yᵀs > 0, guaranteed by the Wolfe conditions
w: yᵀs < 0, guaranteed by the Armijo condition
sᵀs > 1, guaranteed by a unit initial step
yᵀy > 0, guaranteed by any descent direction
questions.x: BFGS preserves positive definiteness when yᵀs > 0, and the Wolfe curvature condition ensures this for every accepted step.

questions.q: Linear CG in exact arithmetic on an n-dimensional quadratic with SPD Hessian converges in
questions.x: CG generates H-conjugate directions, and exact minimization along n mutually conjugate directions reaches the minimizer of an n-dimensional quadratic.

questions.q: In nonlinear CG with p_{k+1} = −g_{k+1} + β_{k+1}p_k, the Fletcher-Reeves β_{k+1} is
questions.x: Fletcher-Reeves uses the ratio of successive squared gradient norms, β_{k+1} = ‖g_{k+1}‖²/‖g_k‖².

questions.q: Which subproblem does a trust region method solve each iteration?
questions.a: min m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp subject to ‖p‖ ≤ Δ
w: min m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp subject to ‖p‖ ≥ Δ
min f(x + p) exactly, subject to the bound ‖p‖ = Δ on the step
min gᵀp subject to pᵀBp ≤ Δ²
questions.x: Each iteration minimizes the quadratic model m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp over the ball ‖p‖ ≤ Δ.

questions.q: The trust region ratio ρ is defined as
questions.x: ρ compares the actual reduction f(x) − f(x+p) with the reduction predicted by the model, m(0) − m(p).

questions.q: A trial step gives ρ = −0.3. What is the standard action?
questions.a: Reject the step and shrink Δ
w: Accept the step and expand Δ
Accept the step and keep Δ unchanged
Reject the step and expand Δ
questions.x: Negative ρ means f increased, so the step is rejected and the trust region radius is reduced.

questions.q: A trial step lies on the boundary (‖p‖ = Δ) and gives ρ = 0.95. What is the standard action?
questions.a: Accept the step and expand Δ
w: Accept the step and shrink Δ
Reject the step and shrink Δ
Accept the step and reset Δ to ‖g‖
questions.x: ρ near 1 with a boundary step shows the model is trustworthy, so the step is accepted and Δ grows (for example doubled).

questions.q: g = (2, 0), B = I, Δ = 10. What is the Cauchy point?
questions.x: Along −g the model minimizer is at α = gᵀg/(gᵀBg) = 1, giving p = (−2, 0), which lies inside Δ = 10.

questions.q: B is positive definite and ‖B⁻¹g‖ ≤ Δ. The trust region (dogleg) step is
w: The midpoint of the dogleg path
questions.x: The unconstrained model minimizer −B⁻¹g lies within the trust region, so it solves the subproblem exactly.

questions.q: Put the dogleg step construction in order (B positive definite)
steps: Compute p_B = −B⁻¹g and take it if ‖p_B‖ ≤ Δ
If ‖p_U‖ ≥ Δ, take the boundary step −Δg/‖g‖
Else move from p_U toward p_B and stop at ‖p‖ = Δ
questions.x: The dogleg path runs from the origin to p_U along −g, then straight to the Newton point p_B, and the step is p_B itself when it fits or the point where the path meets ‖p‖ = Δ.

questions.q: As Δ → 0, the direction of the trust region step approaches
w: The eigenvector of B with largest eigenvalue
questions.x: For small Δ the linear term dominates the model, so the step aligns with −g; for large Δ with B positive definite it approaches the Newton step.

questions.q: Convention: min f subject to h = 0, g ≤ 0, with L = f + λᵀh + μᵀg. Match each KKT condition to its statement
questions.x: With L = f + λᵀh + μᵀg and g ≤ 0, the KKT conditions are stationarity of L, primal feasibility, μ ≥ 0, and μᵢgᵢ = 0.

questions.q: min x² subject to g = 1 − x ≤ 0, with L = f + μg. What is the KKT point?
questions.x: Stationarity 2x − μ = 0 with the active constraint x = 1 gives μ* = 2, which satisfies μ ≥ 0.

questions.q: Convention g ≤ 0. Constraint gᵢ is inactive at x*, so gᵢ(x*) < 0. Then
questions.x: Complementary slackness μᵢgᵢ = 0 sets the multiplier of an inactive constraint to zero, so it drops out of stationarity.

questions.q: Convention min f, g ≤ 0. Geometrically, at a KKT point
questions.a: −∇f lies in the cone spanned by active ∇gᵢ
w: ∇f lies in the cone spanned by active ∇gᵢ
−∇f lies in the cone spanned by inactive ∇gᵢ
questions.x: −∇f = Σμᵢ∇gᵢ with μᵢ ≥ 0 over active constraints, so every feasible direction d has ∇fᵀd ≥ 0 to first order.

questions.q: The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) at x* requires
questions.a: Gradients of active constraints are linearly independent
w: Gradients of all constraints are mutually orthogonal
Gradients of active constraints are linearly dependent
Gradients of all constraints, active and inactive, are independent
questions.x: LICQ holds when the active constraint gradients at x* are linearly independent, which makes the KKT conditions necessary at a local minimizer with unique multipliers.

questions.q: For min f subject to g(x) ≤ c, with L = f + μ(g − c), how does the optimal value f* change with c?
questions.x: Raising c enlarges the feasible set and f* falls at rate μ, so df*/dc = −μ, and a large μ marks a constraint worth relaxing.

questions.q: Second-order sufficient condition at a KKT point (strict complementarity, J = active constraint Jacobian)
questions.a: Zᵀ(∇²L)Z ≻ 0, with Z a basis for null(J)
w: Zᵀ(∇²f)Z ≻ 0, with Z a basis for range(Jᵀ)
Zᵀ(∇²L)Z ≺ 0, with Z a basis for null(J)
∇²f ≻ 0 on all of ℝⁿ, ignoring the constraints
questions.x: Positive definiteness of the Hessian of the Lagrangian on directions tangent to the active constraints, together with the KKT conditions, is sufficient for a strict local minimum.

questions.q: Convention g ≤ 0. At a candidate point an active inequality has μ < 0. What does this mean?
questions.a: Moving off that constraint into the interior lowers f
w: The point is a constrained minimizer with that constraint active
The constraint is redundant and can be deleted
The Hessian of L must be negative definite
questions.x: A negative multiplier means f decreases as x moves off that constraint into the feasible interior, so an active-set method drops it from the active set.

questions.q: min x subject to x ≥ 1, using φ = x + (μ/2)·max(0, 1 − x)². Minimizer of φ for μ = 10?
questions.x: For x < 1, 1 − μ(1 − x) = 0 gives x = 1 − 1/μ = 0.9, on the infeasible side, approaching 1 as μ → ∞.

questions.q: min x subject to x ≥ 1, using the barrier φ = x − μ ln(x − 1). Minimizer of φ for μ = 0.1?
questions.x: 1 − μ/(x − 1) = 0 gives x = 1 + μ = 1.1, strictly feasible, approaching 1 as μ → 0.

questions.q: In a log barrier method, μ is
questions.a: A homotopy parameter driven toward 0 between solves
w: A design variable optimized together with x
A homotopy parameter that is driven toward ∞ between solves
questions.x: μ is held fixed within each subproblem and decreased toward 0 across outer iterations, tracing the central path x*(μ) to the constrained optimum.

questions.q: The central path of an interior point method is
questions.a: The curve of barrier minimizers x*(μ) as μ → 0
w: The curve of exterior penalty minimizers x*(μ) as μ → ∞
The boundary of the feasible region
The steepest descent path from x₀
questions.x: The barrier subproblem minimizers x*(μ) form a smooth curve through the interior of the feasible set that converges to x* as μ → 0.

questions.q: The exact ℓ1 penalty f + ρΣ|hⱼ| + ρΣmax(0, gᵢ) recovers a local minimizer x* for finite ρ when
questions.a: ρ exceeds the largest |multiplier| at x*
w: ρ → ∞ only, like the quadratic penalty
ρ is below the smallest multiplier at the solution x*
ρ equals the norm of ∇f at x*
questions.x: The ℓ1 penalty is exact: any finite ρ above the largest multiplier magnitude makes x* a local minimizer of the penalty function.

questions.q: Why does the quadratic penalty subproblem become hard to minimize as μ grows?
w: The iterates jump to the feasible interior
It becomes nonsmooth at the boundary
questions.x: The penalty Hessian has eigenvalues of order μ along constraint normals and order one along the constraints, so its condition number grows like μ.

questions.q: Each SQP iteration
questions.a: Solves a QP: quadratic model of L, linearized constraints
w: Solves an LP: linear model of f, quadratic constraints
Minimizes an unconstrained penalty with growing μ
Solves a QP: quadratic model of f, exact nonlinear constraints
questions.x: SQP minimizes a quadratic model built from the Hessian of the Lagrangian subject to linearized constraints, which is Newton's method applied to the KKT conditions.

questions.q: Put the steps of a log barrier method (constraints g ≤ 0) in order
steps: Pick a strictly feasible x₀ and an initial μ₀ > 0
Minimize f − μΣln(−gᵢ) for the current μ
Decrease μ, for example μ ← μ/10
Warm start from that minimizer and repeat until μ is small
questions.x: Barrier methods solve a sequence of smooth subproblems with decreasing μ, each warm-started from the last, following the central path to x*.

questions.q: Least squares fit of ŷ = Φw to data y. The normal equations are
questions.x: Minimizing ‖Φw − y‖² gives ΦᵀΦw = Φᵀy, with a unique solution when Φ has full column rank.

questions.q: A full quadratic response surface in 3 variables. Minimum number of distinct samples for a unique least squares fit?
questions.x: A full quadratic in k variables has (k+1)(k+2)/2 terms, which is 10 for k = 3, and full column rank needs at least that many samples.

questions.q: The model ŷ = w₀ + w₁x + w₂x² + w₃ sin x is
questions.a: Linear in the parameters, so linear least squares applies
w: Nonlinear in the parameters, so it needs nonlinear regression
Linear in x, so only a straight line can be fit
Quadratic in the parameters, so it needs Newton's method
questions.x: ŷ is a weighted sum of fixed basis functions of x, so it is linear in w and fits by linear least squares.

questions.q: Ridge regression modifies the normal equations to
questions.x: Ridge adds λ‖w‖² to the least squares loss, giving (ΦᵀΦ + λI)w = Φᵀy, which is well-posed for any λ > 0 and shrinks the weights.

questions.q: What does noise-free kriging (a Gaussian process) provide beyond a polynomial response surface?
questions.a: A variance estimate, zero at the samples
w: A variance estimate, largest at the samples
The exact global optimum of the true function
Reliable accuracy far outside the sampled region
questions.x: Noise-free kriging interpolates the samples and gives a predictive variance that is zero at sample points and grows between them, which drives infill criteria such as expected improvement.

questions.q: Which design of experiments suits a deterministic computer simulation?
questions.a: Latin hypercube or another space-filling design
w: Replicated center points to estimate pure error
Randomized complete blocks to remove nuisance effects
questions.x: A deterministic code returns the same output for the same input, so space-filling designs such as Latin hypercube sampling place every run at a new location; replication and blocking serve noisy physical experiments.

questions.q: How is overfitting of a surrogate best detected?
w: R² computed on the same samples used for fitting
Counting the number of basis functions alone
questions.x: Cross-validation predicts each held-out sample from a model fit to the rest, so it measures generalization error and rises when the model overfits.

questions.q: With n samples and m basis functions, match each surrogate term to its meaning
pairs: R² penalized for the number of terms
Fits derivative data along with function values
questions.x: Least squares handles n > m, regularization such as ridge resolves n < m, adjusted R² charges for extra terms, and gradient-enhanced models use derivative data to reduce the samples needed.

questions.q: For a convex objective on a convex feasible set, any local minimizer is
w: Only a local minimizer in general
questions.x: Convexity makes every local minimizer global, and the set of minimizers is convex (a single point when f is strictly convex).

questions.q: Match each convexity notion to its definition
pairs: Segment between two feasible points stays feasible
questions.x: The chord lies on or above the graph, the tangent lies on or below it, and the Hessian is positive semidefinite, which are equivalent for smooth f; a convex set contains the segment joining any two of its points.

questions.q: The feasible set {x : g(x) ≤ 0} is guaranteed convex when
questions.x: A sublevel set of a convex function is convex, so convex inequality constraints (with affine equalities) give a convex feasible set.

questions.q: Truncation error orders of forward and central finite differences are
questions.x: From the Taylor series, the forward difference error is O(h) and the central difference error is O(h²).

questions.q: Why does shrinking h far below about 10⁻⁸ degrade a double-precision forward difference?
w: Truncation error grows in proportion to 1/h²
The Taylor series diverges as h becomes small
Floating-point overflow in dividing by h
questions.x: f(x+h) and f(x) share nearly all leading digits, so their difference keeps few significant digits and round-off error grows like ε/h.

questions.q: The complex step derivative approximation is
questions.a: f′(x) ≈ Im[f(x + ih)]/h, usable with h ≈ 10⁻²⁰⁰
w: f′(x) ≈ Re[f(x + ih)]/h, usable with h ≈ 10⁻²⁰⁰
f′(x) ≈ Im[f(x + ih) − f(x)]/(2h), with O(h) error
questions.x: The complex step f′(x) ≈ Im[f(x + ih)]/h uses a single evaluation and a division, so h can be tiny (10⁻²⁰⁰) and the derivative is accurate to machine precision.

questions.q: A wing problem has 500 design variables and 2 functions of interest from a CFD solver. Cheapest analytic gradient method?
questions.x: The adjoint method needs one linear solve per function of interest, so 2 solves give gradients with respect to all 500 variables; the direct method needs one solve per design variable.

questions.q: With residuals R(x, u) = 0 and state u, the coefficient matrix of the adjoint linear system is
questions.x: In the convention df/dx = ∂f/∂x − ψᵀ∂R/∂x, the adjoint solves (∂R/∂u)ᵀψ = (∂f/∂u)ᵀ, the transpose of the Jacobian used by the direct method.

Contours are ellipses centred at x*
Principal axes lie along the eigenvectors of H and pass through x*

points: Minimizers exist exactly when b lies in the range of H, so Hx = −b is solvable
Then the minimizers form a line (an affine set) along the null space of H
When b has a component along the null space, f decreases linearly along it and is unbounded below
Check the linear term by projecting b onto the null-space eigenvector

boards.prompt: Write the strong Wolfe conditions and explain the role of each one.
points: Sufficient decrease: f(x+αp) ≤ f(x) + c₁α∇fᵀp bounds the step from above
Strong curvature: |∇f(x+αp)ᵀp| ≤ c₂|∇fᵀp| forces steps long enough to flatten the slope
Constants satisfy 0 < c₁ < c₂ < 1, typically c₁ = 10⁻⁴ and c₂ = 0.9 for quasi-Newton
Wolfe steps ensure yᵀs > 0, keeping BFGS updates positive definite

boards.prompt: Sketch steepest descent with exact line search on an elongated quadratic bowl and explain its convergence rate.
points: Each new gradient is orthogonal to the previous step, giving a zigzag path
Exact step on a quadratic is α = gᵀg/(gᵀHg)
Convergence is linear with factor ((κ−1)/(κ+1))² on f − f*
κ = λ_max/λ_min of the Hessian, so elongated contours mean slow progress
Rescaling variables or using Newton or quasi-Newton directions restores fast convergence

boards.prompt: Compare Newton's method and BFGS in cost, requirements and convergence rate.
points: Newton solves Hp = −g with exact second derivatives and converges quadratically near the solution
Newton needs a positive definite H for descent, so modified Newton uses H + τI
BFGS builds B from gradient differences using the secant condition B_{k+1}s = y
BFGS needs only gradients and converges superlinearly
BFGS stays positive definite when yᵀs > 0, which a Wolfe line search guarantees

boards.prompt: Explain the conjugate gradient method on a quadratic and why it terminates in a finite number of steps.
points: Search directions are H-conjugate: p_iᵀHp_j = 0 for i ≠ j
Each exact line search minimizes f over the subspace spanned by all directions so far
On an n-dimensional quadratic CG reaches the minimizer in at most n iterations in exact arithmetic
New directions are p_{k+1} = −g_{k+1} + βp_k, with Fletcher-Reeves β = ‖g_{k+1}‖²/‖g_k‖²
CG stores only a few vectors, which suits large problems

boards.prompt: Draw one trust region iteration and explain how the radius is updated.
points: The model m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp is minimized subject to ‖p‖ ≤ Δ
ρ = (f(x) − f(x+p))/(m(0) − m(p)) compares actual with predicted reduction
Small ρ (below about 1/4) shrinks Δ
ρ near 1 with a step on the boundary expands Δ
The step is accepted when ρ exceeds a small threshold η

boards.prompt: Sketch the dogleg path and state when the full Newton step is taken.
points: The first leg runs along −g to p_U = −(gᵀg/gᵀBg)g, the model minimizer along steepest descent
The second leg runs straight from p_U to the Newton point p_B = −B⁻¹g
The step is where the path crosses ‖p‖ = Δ
The full Newton step is taken when B is positive definite and ‖p_B‖ ≤ Δ
Along the dogleg ‖p‖ increases and the model value decreases monotonically

boards.prompt: For min f subject to g(x) ≤ 0, draw the geometry at a constrained optimum and write the KKT conditions.
points: Convention: L = f + μᵀg with g ≤ 0
Stationarity ∇f + Σμᵢ∇gᵢ = 0 puts −∇f in the cone of active constraint gradients
Dual feasibility μᵢ ≥ 0 and complementary slackness μᵢgᵢ = 0, so inactive constraints carry zero multipliers
LICQ (linearly independent active gradients) makes the multipliers unique
Second-order check: the reduced Hessian of L is positive definite on the active-constraint tangent space

boards.prompt: What is the physical meaning of a Lagrange multiplier in a design problem?
points: The multiplier is the sensitivity of the optimal objective to the constraint limit (a shadow price)
For g(x) ≤ c with L = f + μ(g − c), df*/dc = −μ
A large multiplier marks the constraint that most limits the design
Inactive constraints have μ = 0 and zero first-order effect on f*

boards.prompt: Contrast an exterior quadratic penalty with an interior log barrier on a single inequality constraint g ≤ 0.
points: The penalty adds (μ/2)·max(0, g)², and its minimizers approach x* from the infeasible side as μ → ∞
The barrier adds −μ ln(−g), iterates stay strictly feasible, and μ → 0
μ is a homotopy parameter held fixed within each subproblem
Barrier minimizers trace the central path x*(μ)
Both subproblems grow ill-conditioned at the limit of μ, which motivates exact ℓ1 penalties, SQP and primal-dual interior point methods

boards.prompt: Describe sequential quadratic programming and compare it with an interior point method.
points: SQP solves a QP each iteration: a quadratic model of the Lagrangian with linearized constraints
SQP is Newton's method on the KKT conditions and converges quickly near the solution
A merit function such as the exact ℓ1 penalty, or a filter, globalizes SQP
Interior point methods treat inequalities with a barrier and follow the central path
Interior point methods scale well to many inequality constraints; SQP excels when function evaluations are expensive

boards.prompt: You have budget for 40 runs of a CFD code in 5 variables. How do you choose the samples, build a surrogate and validate it?
points: Use a space-filling design such as Latin hypercube sampling, since the code is deterministic
A full quadratic in 5 variables has 21 terms, so 40 samples give an overdetermined least squares fit
Solve ΦᵀΦw = Φᵀy, which has a unique solution when Φ has full column rank
Check accuracy with cross-validation and adjusted R²
Use predictions only inside the sampled region, since extrapolation is risky

boards.prompt: When would you choose kriging or radial basis functions over a polynomial response surface?
points: Kriging and RBFs interpolate deterministic data and capture multimodal behaviour
Kriging provides a predictive variance, zero at the samples and larger between them
That variance drives adaptive sampling such as expected improvement
Polynomial response surfaces suit smooth, low-order trends and noisy data
Gradient-enhanced kriging uses derivative data to reduce the number of samples needed

boards.prompt: You need gradients of drag and lift with respect to 200 shape variables from a CFD solver. Which method do you use and why?
points: The governing equations are residuals R(x, u) = 0 for the state u
The direct method costs one linear solve per design variable
The adjoint method costs one linear solve per function of interest, independent of the number of design variables
Here the adjoint needs 2 solves versus 200 for the direct method, so the adjoint is the choice
Finite differences need about 200 extra analyses and a careful step size choice

boards.prompt: Define convexity and explain why it matters in design optimization.
points: Zeroth order: the chord lies on or above the graph, f(θx + (1−θ)y) ≤ θf(x) + (1−θ)f(y)
First order: the tangent lies on or below the graph, f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x)
Second order: ∇²f is positive semidefinite everywhere
A convex problem has a convex objective and a convex feasible set, such as convex g ≤ 0 with affine h = 0
For a convex problem every local minimizer is a global minimizer
